list.listitem: Advise parents to use "Back to Sleep" for every sleep. This means using a firm, non-inclined sleep surface without loose bedding or other soft objects in the same room but not sharing a bed with the mother or caregiver. Avoid overheating and overbundling. A

Women should seek and obtain regular prenatal care during pregnancy, as this reduces risk of SIDS, with breastfeeding encouraged. Smoke exposure and use of alcohol and illicit drugs during and after pregnancy should be avoided. A
Infants should receive immunizations following CDC recommendations. A
Do not use home cardiorespiratory monitors as a strategy to reduce the risk of SIDS. A
In cases of sudden/unexpected infant death, a thorough case investigation is needed, including a complete autopsy, examination of the death scene, and review of the clinical history. C

background.definition: The sudden death of an infant under 1 year of age that remains unexplained after a thorough case investigation, including performance of a complete autopsy, examination of the death scene, and review of the clinical history.

list.listitem: United States: 0.56 deaths per 1000 live births in 2001 (decreased dramatically from 1.37/1000 in 1987 and 1.2/1000 in 1992, before the Back to Sleep campaign began in 1994). Relatively constant from 2001 to 2008 (0.54/1000), then further decrease to 0.40/1000 in 2013.
Despite a decrease of more than 50% since the early 1990s, SIDS remains the leading cause of death from age 28 days to 1 year.
2 to 2.5 times more common among black infants than white infants.
Varies worldwide (as low as 0.046/1000 in Hong Kong to as high as 6.7/1000 in American Indians/Alaska Natives).
Peak incidence between 2 and 4 months (median age 11 weeks).
90% of SIDS before 6 months of age.
Most common cause of infant death in the United States beyond the neonatal period.
See Risk Factors and Protective Factors table.
By definition, the cause is unknown.
It is thought that SIDS may be caused by congenital abnormalities in cardiopulmonary control and external stressors. However, the precise mechanism has not been fully defined.
See table for risk factors and protective factors that may represent those external stressors.

list.listitem: Primary care providers should actively engage in and promote the "Safe to Sleep" campaign. Infants should be placed for sleep in a supine position, every time. Side sleeping is not advised.
Use a firm, non-inclined sleep surface (a firm crib mattress, covered by a sheet), without soft materials or objects under or around the sleeping infant.
Keep soft objects and loose bedding out of the crib (e.g., pillows, loose blankets, stuffed animals).

Avoid overheating by clothing the infant lightly for sleep, maintaining the bedroom temperature at a comfortable level for a lightly clothed adult, avoiding overbundling, and ensuring that the infant does not feel hot to the touch.
There is no evidence to support swaddling as a means of reducing risk of SIDS.
Do not smoke during pregnancy or after birth. Avoid other sources of smoke exposure as well.
Do not use alcohol or other illicit substances during pregnancy or after birth.

Infants should sleep in the same room as the mother.
However, parents/caregivers should not share the same sleep surface (bed, couch, etc.) with an infant.

Consider offering a pacifier at nap time and bedtime when placing the infant to sleep, throughout the first year of life. For breast-fed infants, delay pacifier introduction until 1 month of age to ensure that breast-feeding is well established.
Recommend supervised, awake tummy time, which facilitates development and reduces positional plagiocephaly.
Avoid devices marketed to reduce the risk of SIDS—there is no evidence that such devices are safe or reduce risk of SIDS.
Do not use home cardiorespiratory monitors as a strategy to reduce the risk of SIDS.

Expand the campaign to reduce the risk of SIDS. Primary care providers are encouraged to participate. Public education should target all caregivers of infants (including child care providers, grandparents, foster parents, babysitters, and others). Education should include efforts to overcome behavior change. Continue a special focus on the black and American Indian/Native Alaskan populations.

Regular prenatal care during pregnancy reduces risk of SIDS. Also, encourage immunization (following recommendations of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and/or regional immunization schedules/recommendations).
SIDS risk reduction recommendations should be promoted and modeled by child care providers and health care providers, including staff in newborn nurseries and NICUs. A
In the event of sudden or unexpected infant death, perform a thorough case investigation.
Investigation should include complete autopsy, examination of the death scene, and review of the clinical history.
SIDS is only diagnosed when no cause of death is identified.
